doc.title: Jake Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Playing on top of or behind the beat
summary: Hanna says laying back means dragging; Basie's band played right on time.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: A couple of times the subject has come up about playing on top of the beat, playing behind the beat. Does such a thing exist?

Well if you play on the top you rush. If you play behind you drag. Now if the rhythm did that, if they laid back, they’d be dragging see? If the band goes, “Well we’re going to lay back.” “Well we’ll join you.” “Oh, no, no, no, it’ll slow down.” And everybody played right in tempo, like Count Basie does. Basie’s band, do they lay back? I says no they don’t. Play the records you can hear the rhythm drop out. They go swinging straight ahead. Basie never allowed that. He always had Sweets Edison, Buck Clayton and they were right on the money man. Snooky Young. The best, the best. Oh, Lester Young. You know, who’s better than those guys? The guys were right on time. Man, they don’t lay back of the beat. They’re dragging, that’s all that is. You can’t get swinging if you do that. You can’t get swinging if you double time the medium tempos either. Those guys were always swinging. The band was always swinging. They were right on the money, right on time.
